#### 01. Construction marketplace — Web app

https://veilvex.pages.dev/cases/mybuild/

A two-sided platform: the client publishes a construction order, companies bid with a price and a deadline, and the deal moves step by step through to acceptance. Two dashboards, real-time updates, files and notifications.

- **Result**: Orders, bids and work acceptance in one platform
- **Timeline**: 4 months of development
- **Cost**: ≈ $26,500
- **Stack & channels**: Next.js, NestJS, PostgreSQL, WebSocket

**01. About the project**

The client’s name and project data are covered by a non-disclosure agreement, so this page describes how the platform works rather than whom it serves. A public demo on test data is built from the same code as the production system.

**02. The problem**

Before the platform, the client and the construction company negotiated over chat and by phone. Deal terms got lost in messages, drawings and estimates were scattered across conversations, and neither side could say precisely what stage the work was at.

They needed a system where a deal has explicit steps, every step is confirmed by both sides, and none of them can be skipped.

**03. What we built**

- Two dashboards in one application: the client manages their orders; the construction company sees the feed of available orders, its own bids and its work submissions.
- An order form with category, property type, floor area, address, budget, preferred start date and files: drawings and plans are attached upfront, so the company prices the job from documents rather than from a verbal description.
- Bids with a price and a deadline: the client sees them side by side and picks one. The deal price and deadline are taken from the accepted bid, and the remaining bids automatically move to “not selected”.
- Work submission with files and a mandatory comment, acceptance by the client, and sending work back for revision with a new submission round. The history of every round is kept.
- Real-time updates: an action on one side appears on the other without reloading the page.
- Notifications for every event in the deal, with an unread counter.
- A contractor directory showing the number of completed orders, plus a Documents section with every file across every order.
- Private file storage: a download link lives for five minutes and is issued only to someone entitled to that file.
- Dark and light themes, responsive from phone to large screen.

**04. How the deal works**

An order status cannot be set by hand. Every permitted transition is described in a single table, and any action outside it is rejected with a clear explanation. Status, bids and notifications change within one transaction, so the state of the deal cannot drift apart between the two sides’ screens.

1. Looking for a contractor — the order is published, no bids yet.
2. Awaiting confirmation — at least one bid has arrived, the client is choosing.
3. In progress — a bid is accepted, price and deadline are fixed.
4. Awaiting completion confirmation — the company has submitted the work with files and a comment.
5. Under revision — the client sent the work back, the company prepares the next submission round.
6. Completed — the client accepted the work.

**05. What an outside company sees**

Privacy here is a rule built into the data itself, not a footnote. A company that is not part of the deal sees the order as “looking for a contractor”, whatever its real state. It sees neither the deal price, nor other companies’ bids, nor the client’s contacts.

The same rule applies in three places at once: in the server response, in the addressing of real-time events and in file access.

**06. Technology**

Next.js and React on the interface side, NestJS and PostgreSQL on the server side, TypeScript throughout. Real-time updates run over WebSocket; authentication and file storage are on Supabase.

The shared rules of the deal live in a separate package used by both sides, so the button on screen and the check on the server are computed by one and the same function and cannot diverge.

**07. Timeline and cost**

Four months of development, followed by acceptance testing on the client side. Project cost: about $26,500.

#### 02. English courses — Paid ads

https://veilvex.pages.dev/cases/target-english-courses/

Targeted ads for an online English school: the audience was widened to the CIS countries, traffic was split between the website and Instagram, and a chatbot took over the frequent questions.

- **Result**: 95 applications in 10 days
- **Period**: 10 days, April 2024
- **Cost per click**: $0.03
- **Stack & channels**: Targeting, Instagram, Chatbot

**01. The goal**

An online English school needed more course applications — through Instagram and through its website.

**02. What we did**

- Widened the geography: the audience was initially limited to one city, but the school is online and a student’s location is irrelevant — so we added the CIS countries.
- Split traffic into two scenarios: visits to the school’s website and direct messages on Instagram.
- Connected a chatbot that handles prospective students’ frequent questions and moves them on to the school’s site — a manager joins an already warm conversation.
- Used both our own creatives and posts that were already performing on the account.

**03. Results over 10 days**

- **95** — applications
- **$1.35** — average cost per enquiry ($0.57 to $2.95 depending on the audience)
- **9.3%** — click-through rate on website ads
- **$0.03** — cost per click to the website

**04. Why it matters**

This is a clear example of why one number never tells the story: a direct message costs more than a site visit, but it also behaves differently. Splitting traffic into two scenarios, plus a chatbot absorbing routine questions, gave the school a steady flow of applications on a controlled budget. The campaign ran in April 2024.

#### 06. Yakitori — Website

https://veilvex.pages.dev/cases/yakitori-site/ · Visit the live site: https://yakitori.az/

A menu website for an Asian restaurant: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no CMS and no build step, two language versions as separate pages, menu sections rendered from data, sticky navigation and a lightbox.

- **Result**: A 15-section menu site in two languages
- **Timeline**: ≈ 1 week
- **Launched**: 17 August 2026
- **Stack & channels**: HTML/CSS/JS, Zero dependencies, Multilingual, SEO, JSON-LD Restaurant, Cloudflare Pages

**01. About the client**

Yakitori · Asian Food is an Asian restaurant: sushi and rolls, soups, noodles, fried rice, udon, tempura, salads, waffles, ice cream and drinks, plus delivery across the city. A guest comes to a site like this for one thing: to read the menu with prices and call. That means the site has to open instantly on a phone and show a dish as a photograph, not as a line in a list.

**02. What we did**

- Built the site in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript: no CMS, no bundler, not a single external dependency. Pages are served as finished files, an update is a folder copy, and there are no plugins to break on the next release.
- Separated data from rendering. The entire menu lives in one data file, and a script builds both the card grid and the section navigation from it. Changing a price or an ingredient list never touches the markup.
- Shipped the two language versions as separate pages rather than a client-side switcher: Russian on yakitori.az, Azerbaijani on yakitori.az/az. Each has its own canonical and a full hreflang cluster (ru, az and x-default): a search engine sees two self-contained documents, not one document swapping its text.
- Laid the menu out across 15 sections — from sets and combos to lemonades — with five groups inside sushi and rolls: hosomaki, uramaki, hot rolls, baked rolls, and the sushi burger with rice balls. The last three sections are typeset as a price list and fold into columns automatically.
- Built sticky section navigation: the active item is highlighted by an IntersectionObserver, the strip scrolls with the wheel and drags with the mouse, and a click right after a drag is suppressed — otherwise dragging would randomly jump to another section.
- Added a lightbox: clicking any photo opens it full screen; any click or the Escape key closes it.
- Cropped the dish photography in CSS only, without touching the files. For the soups, scale and focal point are tuned so the bowls come out the same size across a row; the lightbox still opens the untouched original.
- Wrote the full search markup: title, description, canonical, hreflang, geo metadata, Open Graph and a Twitter card, and JSON-LD Restaurant with the phone, address, opening hours, coordinates and price range.
- Converted every raster image to WebP and deployed to Cloudflare Pages; the www address redirects to the main one, which keeps the QR code on the printed flyer working — the www form is what went to press.

**03. Design and structure**

The site runs on the brand’s two themes. The dark one covers the header, the first screen and the footer: dark brown ground, cream text, gold lettering and a red rule under the header. The light one carries the menu itself: cream paper with a seigaiha pattern, white dish cards, red prices. The result reads as a printed menu card laid on a dark cover — exactly what the restaurant is.

The first screen is not an advert: a headline, one sentence, an order button and two lines of facts — opening hours and the address. The phone number sits in the header and again in the footer, because orders here come by phone, not through a cart.

**04. Typography and the Azerbaijani version**

Three typefaces, and no fourth: Montserrat for headings, dish names and prices, Manrope for ingredient lists and descriptions, Noto Sans JP for the Japanese section labels. The split is not decorative: Manrope physically lacks the local currency sign and the Azerbaijani letter Ə, so every price is set in Montserrat, and Manrope falls back to that same Montserrat — it is what draws the Ə inside Azerbaijani dish descriptions.

Without it the browser would silently fall back to a system font: CSS gives no sign of this, the family is assigned and everything “works”, yet the letter drops out of the line. We checked it with a script rather than by eye: it asks the browser which real font rendered each text node on both pages.

The second Azerbaijani trap is casing. A plain uppercase transform turns i into I, while Azerbaijani needs İ, so every string that renders in caps is already stored capitalised in the data and the transform stays a no-op.

**05. How the site behaves on a phone**

Most orders come in from a phone, so the menu grid was checked across fourteen widths, from a wide monitor down to a narrow handset. One rule sits behind all of them: a dish name must never break onto a second line and collide with its price.

- On a tablet the grid is forced into two columns.
- On a phone the price drops below the name instead of sharing a line with it.
- On the narrowest screens the whole text steps down a size.

Sizes were tuned to Montserrat: at the same size it runs about a fifth wider than Manrope, so eyeballing does not work here.

**06. Timeline and process**

About a week of work. The site went live at yakitori.az on 17 August 2026, and the project closed on 18 August together with the flyer: the flyer carries a QR code pointing to the site, so the two could not be signed off separately.

#### 08. Deniz Service — Website

https://veilvex.pages.dev/cases/deniz-service/ · Visit the live site: https://denizservice.com/

A bilingual site for an industrial supplier: a 21-category catalogue with anchor navigation, a purpose-built certificates component, clean URLs on Apache and full search markup.

- **Result**: Supplier catalogue: 21 categories and documents one click away
- **Timeline**: ≈ 2 weeks
- **Delivered**: July 2026
- **Stack & channels**: HTML/CSS/JS, jQuery, Multilingual, SEO, Apache/.htaccess

**01. About the client**

Deniz Service has provided supply and engineering support since 2005: oil and gas, metallurgy, the food and chemical industries, construction and agriculture. It works as a single point of procurement — from explosion-proof equipment and valves to rigging, HVAC and personal protective equipment — and represents eleven foreign manufacturers in Azerbaijan. The company holds an ISO 9001:2015 quality management certificate and a D-U-N-S registration.

A business like this does not need a site that sells in one click: an engineer or a procurement officer arrives to check two things — whether the range covers what they need, and whether the supplier is authorised to supply it.

**02. What we did**

- Built the site on plain code — HTML, CSS, JavaScript and jQuery, with no CMS: pages are served as ready files, so there is nothing to break on a plugin update and no admin panel to attack.
- Shipped two language versions: English at the root, Azerbaijani under /az/. Every page carries its own canonical and a full hreflang cluster — en, az and x-default.
- Moved the catalogue onto its own page: 21 product and service categories, each broken down into what it includes. Cards on the homepage link by anchor straight into the relevant block instead of the top of a long list.
- Wrote the Partners section component from scratch: a strip of eleven brands is generated from a single data file, and a click opens a custom lightbox — click and wheel zoom, pinch on phones, drag with a threshold (so a click never turns into an accidental nudge), vertical thumbnails and support for brands with more than one authorisation document.
- Configured Apache through .htaccess: URLs without .html, 301 redirects from the old forms, forced HTTPS, the non-www address and no trailing slash — exactly one canonical form per page. The same file handles gzip, cache headers by file type, security headers and correct MIME types for WebP and fonts.
- Wrote the markup search engines read: a JSON-LD @graph with Organization, WebSite, WebPage and BreadcrumbList nodes, Open Graph and Twitter cards, and a sitemap.xml with language alternates on every URL.
- Published the documents directly: the company presentation, the ISO certificate, laboratory accreditations and authorisation letters from all eleven manufacturers. Each PDF opens in one click, with no form and no sign-up.
- Converted all raster graphics to WebP and enabled lazy loading for images.

**03. Design and structure**

The design was developed together with the client. The opening screen is dark, with a production photograph and a single sentence about the company: an industrial supplier gains more from naming its profile immediately than from a slogan. Below sits a grid of light cards on a dark background — 21 categories that read as a catalogue rather than an advertising block.

The graphic motif, a thin mesh of polyhedra across the background images, keeps the engineering tone without competing with the equipment photography. The trust arguments are gathered in one place: years in business, company principles, the ISO certificate and the D-U-N-S mark. Contacts are direct email and phone links next to a map — a procurement officer wants to get in touch, not fill in a form.

**04. Timeline and process**

About two weeks for markup, catalogue content, the certificates component and hosting setup. Delivered in July 2026.

#### 12. Yakitori menu — Design

https://veilvex.pages.dev/cases/yakitori-menu/

A printed A4 menu book across 10 sheets: 68 items with photography, two language versions built from one layout, an editable PPTX for the restaurant and a print PDF with the type converted to outlines.

- **Result**: An A4 menu book: 10 sheets, 68 items, RU and AZ
- **Timeline**: 5 days
- **Delivered**: 10 August 2026
- **Stack & channels**: HTML/CSS, PPTX, Print PDF, Type as outlines, RU / AZ

**01. About the client**

Yakitori · Asian Food is an Asian restaurant. A printed menu on the table is not just a list: the guest holds it for several minutes and chooses by the photograph. What was needed was a book covering the full range, in two languages at once, delivered so that the restaurant could edit the text itself and the printer could go to press without touch-ups.

**02. What we did**

- Laid out an A4 menu book across 10 sheets: five physical sheets, double-sided, spiral bound. It carries 68 items, each with its own photograph — 77 shots in total, with no empty slots.
- Built both language sets, Russian and Azerbaijani, from one layout. The Azerbaijani book is not a fork: the markup, the styles and the converter are shared, and only the text file is separate. Three safety checks fail the build if the source structure drifts, if a service key appears a different number of times than declared, or if visible Russian text is left on a finished page.
- Delivered an editable PowerPoint rather than flat images: the restaurant changes a price or a name itself, without coming back to us.
- Generated the deck from measurements of the rendered page rather than from constants. Box coordinates, text with line breaks already resolved and image paths are read off the drawn layout, so a layout edit travels into the PPTX by itself.
- Cropped the photography with a parameter in the data instead of in an image editor: one formula becomes CSS for the layout and a source rectangle for PowerPoint, so the crop matches in both and the original files stay untouched.
- Produced three print variants for different bindings — spiral, no spiral and a 12-page version — generated by script from a single source, with no duplicated project files.

**03. Design and structure**

The cover is dark and the inner sheets are light: cream paper with a momiji leaf background, dark ink, red accents and gold hairlines. The header and footer of every sheet stay dark, so the book reads as one object rather than a set of unrelated pages.

Each spread has its own card archetype matched to the type of dish: a tile with the photo on top for the sets, a round photo in a white frame with a gold ring for rolls and soups, a large card with the photo on the left for hot rolls, a tilted polaroid for the combos, and a typographic price list for the drinks. The last sheet closes with a round hanko seal reading “Enjoy your meal”.

Some decisions came from the client mid-project, and they changed the layout noticeably. White panels behind the cards took up around 70% of a sheet and hid the leaf background — they were rejected. A card is now translucent glass with a gold hairline, the background shows through it, and the price sits as a tag in the top right corner. The decorative kumiko corners went for the same reason: the sheet became calmer.

One more rule came out of the layout itself: row heights are never hand-tuned, the sections stretch on their own and fill the sheet down to the footer. The worst remaining slack after the spiral margins is under a centimetre, on the sets sheet.

**04. Print**

- Mirrored margins for the spiral: 12.2 mm on the binding side and 6.6 mm on the outer one. The front of a sheet keeps the spiral on the left, the back on the right.
- The logo and phone numbers moved down from the top edge, from 2.9 mm to 6.3–6.6 mm: the original figure was inside the trim tolerance and the printer asked for more room.
- Type delivered as outlines: the finished PDF embeds zero fonts. We verified it with a number, not by eye — “the text can be selected with the mouse” proves nothing here, since a lookup table is written alongside the outlines purely for search and copying.
- A gradient with transparency over a photograph does not survive press: the darkening on the cover came back from the printer flooded magenta. We baked the darkening into the image itself and the problem disappeared.
- The PDF is assembled by our own script rather than saved out of PowerPoint: PowerPoint writes real text with embedded fonts and recompresses the images — the background arrived at roughly 110 dpi against a 300 dpi requirement.

**05. Timeline and process**

Five days of work. The menu was approved, produced and printed, and the work closed on 10 August 2026. The final package: six print PDFs for three binding options, plus two editable PPTX files in Russian and Azerbaijani.

### FAQ — Frequently asked questions

**What is GEO and why does my business need it?**
More and more people don’t scroll search results — they ask AI for advice. GEO is work on your website, content and brand mentions so that AI assistants understand your business and recommend it in their answers.

**What does the price depend on?**
On scope and complexity: number of pages, roles and statuses in an app, integrations, ad platforms. We give an exact estimate after a short brief — it takes about 15 minutes.

**Is the ad budget included in the price?**
No. You pay the ad budget to the platform directly — usually from $200 per month; for Google Ads it can be higher because of keyword costs.

**When will the ads start paying off?**
Ads usually take 3–6 months to ramp up: during this time we find the combinations that consistently bring leads. We don’t promise an instant flood of clients — we promise transparency and weekly reports.

**Can you improve my current website instead of building a new one?**
Yes. We start with an audit and honestly tell you what can be fixed in place and what is cheaper to rebuild. We also support websites built by others.

**Do you work under a contract?**
Yes, always under an official contract. For large projects payment is split into stages — you pay for accepted results, not everything upfront.

**Do you work with clients from other countries?**
Yes. We are not tied to one country: we run projects remotely worldwide in English, Russian, Azerbaijani and German.

### Privacy policy

https://veilvex.pages.dev/privacy/ — Last updated 2026-10-27

The short version: this site uses no advertising or analytics cookies, tracking pixels or third-party counters, and receives from you only what you send us yourself through the request form, plus the technical data no website can work without. Below are the details: exactly what we receive, on what legal basis, who we share it with, how long we keep it and how to exercise your rights.

1. **Who we are and how to reach us**
   Veilvex is the team that runs this website and provides the services presented on it: search and AI visibility (SEO and GEO), advertising, social media, website and app development, AI automation and design. “We” in this policy means Veilvex.
   The controller of your personal data is the owner of the Veilvex brand. If you sign a contract with us, it names the company or sole trader that is your contracting party and is responsible for processing data within our work together. Full legal details are available on request.
   We have not appointed a data protection officer. You can send any request about your data through any current contact listed in this section or on the site: by email, if one is listed, or to the official Veilvex account in Telegram or WhatsApp. If you write in a messenger, we will check that the request comes from the same person who sent the original request (see section 9).
   Formal notices, including under a contract, can be sent through any of these contacts or by email to the address published on this website or in your contract.
2. **What this policy covers**
   This policy applies to every language version of the site, to the request form and to any correspondence with us before a contract is signed — whether through the form, a messenger or email.
   If we work on your project and get access to your customers’ data, that is governed by our contract with you (see section 14). How we work with clients is described in our Terms of Service.
3. **What data we receive**
   From the request form — only what you type in yourself:
   - your name, so we know how to address you;
   - a contact for getting back to you — a phone number, WhatsApp or a Telegram username;
   - the services you selected and, optionally, a short description of the task;
   - the consent checkbox and the language of the page the request was sent from.
   Along with the request, your browser sends two technical fields used to stop bots: a hidden field that people leave empty, and the time the form was opened. Neither contains any information about you.
   If you write to us directly on WhatsApp, Telegram or by email, we see what the messenger shows us: your profile name and photo, your number or username, and your messages.
   Technical data. Like any server on the internet, our hosting receives your IP address, browser details, the requested page and the time with every request. When you submit the form, our handler also (1) computes a cryptographic hash of your IP address and keeps it, with the times of recent submissions, for a short technical window to protect against spam and limit how often requests can be sent, and (2) logs technical events: a shortened fragment of that hash, the language, the number of services selected, the delivery channel and error codes. Your name, contact and message never appear in the logs.
   We do not ask for — and ask you not to send through the form — special categories of data (health, beliefs and the like), identity documents or payment details. Nothing can be paid for on this site.
4. **Cookies, analytics and third parties**
   This site uses no advertising or analytics cookies, tracking pixels, third-party visitor counters, advertising identifiers or browser fingerprinting.
   Your browser may still use technical local storage — for example, to remember the interface language you chose or other technical settings. Such entries are needed only for the site to work, stay on your device, are not used for tracking, and can be cleared in your browser settings. Strictly necessary storage needs no consent, which is why there is no cookie banner.
   Our Content Security Policy (CSP) restricts the loading of third-party scripts that we have not allowed.
   The WhatsApp and Telegram links are plain links: those services receive data only when you follow them, and their own terms apply from then on.
5. **Purposes and legal bases**
   We process data only for the purposes listed below. Legal bases are given under the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR); for other countries, see section 10.
   - Purpose: Reply to your request, run the brief, prepare an estimate and a contract; Data: Form data, correspondence; Legal basis: Steps taken at your request before entering into a contract — Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR; the consent given in the form — Art. 6(1)(a), where the law requires consent
   - Purpose: Perform the contract and run the project; Data: Contact details of client representatives, project correspondence; Legal basis: Contract — Art. 6(1)(b); for employees of a corporate client — legitimate interest, Art. 6(1)(f)
   - Purpose: Protect the form from spam and abuse, keep the site running and secure; Data: IP hash, submission times, technical logs; Legal basis: Legitimate interest in operating a secure website — Art. 6(1)(f)
   - Purpose: Keep accounting and tax records; Data: Contract, invoices, acceptance certificates; Legal basis: Legal obligation — Art. 6(1)(c)
   - Purpose: Defend our rights in a dispute; Data: Contract and project correspondence; Legal basis: Legitimate interest — Art. 6(1)(f)
   Filling in the form is optional — you can simply message us instead. Without a name and a contact, however, we cannot reply.
   We send no marketing emails without your separate consent, we do not sell data, and we do not use requests to train AI models.
6. **Who receives your data**
   Requests are seen only by the members of the Veilvex team who need them to reply and to work on the project. Contractors we bring into a project receive only what they need and are bound by confidentiality obligations.
   Services the data passes through:
   - Cloudflare, Inc. (USA) — website hosting, the form handler, the rate-limit store and technical logs;
   - Telegram — a bot delivers the request to the team’s private chat;
   - Resend, Inc. (USA) — delivers the request as an email to the team’s mailbox, where it is stored by our email provider;
   - WhatsApp (Meta) and Telegram — if you message us there yourself.
   A request arrives via Telegram, by email or both — depending on which channels are enabled. It has no other recipients.
   We disclose data to public authorities only when the law requires it. We never sell or rent out data.
7. **International transfers**
   Cloudflare and Resend are based in the USA, and Telegram operates servers in several countries. Your data may therefore be processed outside your country, including outside the EU/EEA.
   For transfers from the EU/EEA, the UK and Switzerland we rely on adequacy decisions (in particular the EU–U.S. Data Privacy Framework, for recipients certified under it) or on the European Commission’s Standard Contractual Clauses (Art. 46(2)(c) GDPR) built into the providers’ data processing agreements. Where neither applies — for example, when you choose a messenger to contact us — data is transferred only to the extent needed to answer your request (Art. 49(1)(b) GDPR).
   You can ask for a copy of the relevant safeguards using the contacts in section 1.
8. **How long we keep data**
   - Data: Request and correspondence, if no contract follows; Retention: For as long as the discussion is relevant and there is a chance we will return to the task. After that we delete it as part of our periodic clean-up of archives — or sooner, at your request.
   - Data: Contract correspondence and documents; Retention: For the term of the contract, then as long as accounting and tax law requires and until limitation periods expire — usually 3 to 10 years, depending on the country.
   - Data: IP hash and submission times; Retention: Kept only for a short technical window to protect against spam and limit how often requests can be sent. The record holds no request content and is cleared automatically when the technical window expires.
   - Data: Hosting and form-handler logs; Retention: A limited period under Cloudflare’s rules. They contain no request content.
   If you ask us to delete your data sooner, we will — except for anything the law requires us to keep.
9. **Your rights**
   At any time you can:
   - find out what data we hold about you and get a copy of it;
   - have inaccurate or incomplete data corrected;
   - have your data erased (the “right to be forgotten”);
   - restrict processing — for example, while we look into an objection;
   - receive the data you gave us in a machine-readable format, or have it sent to someone else (portability);
   - object to processing based on our legitimate interest;
   - withdraw your consent — this does not affect processing carried out before the withdrawal;
   - lodge a complaint with a data protection authority — in the country where you live or work, or where you believe your rights were infringed.
   How to do it: write to us through any current contact listed in section 1 or on the site — by email, if one is listed, or to the official Veilvex account in Telegram or WhatsApp. To avoid handing your data to someone else, we will check that the request comes from the person who sent the original request — for example, by asking you to write from the contact given in that request or to confirm its details. There is no charge.
   We reply without undue delay and within one month at the latest. For complex or numerous requests this can be extended by two further months; if so, we will tell you within the first month and explain why.
10. **Country-specific information**
   EU, EEA, UK and Switzerland. This policy follows the GDPR, the UK GDPR and the Swiss Federal Act on Data Protection (revFADP). For Germany: the site may store on your device only what is strictly necessary to provide the page you requested (for example, your chosen language); no consent is needed for this under § 25 TDDDG.
   California (CCPA/CPRA), to the extent it applies to us. In the past 12 months we have collected identifiers (name, contact), details of your request and internet activity data (section 3), from the sources and for the purposes described in sections 3 and 5. We do not sell personal information, do not share it for cross-context behavioural advertising and do not use sensitive personal information. You have the right to know what we collect, to have it deleted or corrected, and not to be discriminated against for exercising your rights.
   Azerbaijan. Data is processed in accordance with the Law of the Republic of Azerbaijan “On Personal Data”. Ticking the box in the form is your consent to the processing of the data you provide in order to answer your request, including its transfer abroad to the services listed in section 6. You have the right to know what data about you is processed and how, to have it corrected or destroyed, and to withdraw your consent.
   Other countries. If you are in a country whose law requires separate consent to the processing of personal data and its cross-border transfer in order to answer your request, ticking the box in the form or sending us a message in a messenger confirms that consent. You can withdraw it through the contacts in section 1 and exercise your rights as described in section 9.
11. **Children**
   Our services are meant for businesses and adults. We do not knowingly collect data from anyone under 16. If you believe a child has sent us their data, let us know and we will delete it.
12. **How we protect data**
   - the site is served over HTTPS only, and the HSTS header stops browsers from opening it over an insecure connection;
   - a Content Security Policy (CSP) that restricts the loading of third-party scripts we have not allowed and blocks embedding the site in other pages;
   - the form accepts requests only from our own pages; the server checks every field, rejects unknown ones, strips invisible control characters and caps the request size;
   - submissions are rate-limited, and bots are filtered out by a hidden field and a timing check;
   - requests are delivered as plain text — what you type never becomes HTML markup, either on the site or in the message to the team;
   - IP addresses are stored only as hashes, and service credentials only in protected environment variables, never in the code;
   - only team members who need it for their work can access the chat and mailbox where requests arrive.
   No system on the internet is perfectly secure. If a breach occurs that is likely to put your rights at risk, we will notify the supervisory authority within the statutory deadline and, where required, you as well.
13. **Automated decision-making**
   We do not make decisions based solely on automated processing that have legal or similarly significant effects on you, and we do not profile you. People read and handle every request; the only automation is the spam filter.
14. **Data in client projects**
   When we set up advertising, a CRM, chatbots or analytics, or build a website, we may get access to your customers’ data. In that case you remain the controller and we act as your processor: we handle the data only on your instructions and for the purposes of the project.
   On request we sign a data processing agreement (DPA, Art. 28 GDPR) or include those terms in the contract. We use access to your accounts only for the work, never pass it on, and return it or ask you to revoke it when the project ends.
   As the owner of the website or business, you are responsible for the legal basis for processing your customers’ data, your own privacy policy and consent banners. We will help you prepare and set all of this up technically, but that is not a substitute for legal advice.
15. **Changes to this policy**
   We update this policy when the site, the services we use or the law change. The current version and its date are always published on this page. This policy is published in several languages; English is the default language of this website, and if the versions differ, the English version prevails. A new version takes effect when it is published on this page, unless the version itself states otherwise.

1. **General**
   These terms describe how Veilvex provides its services: search and AI visibility (SEO and GEO), advertising, social media, website and app development, AI automation, design and branding. They apply to requests, negotiations and projects unless the contract says otherwise.

   Our contracting party is the company or sole trader named in the contract. We share its legal details before signing.
   Veilvex services are intended exclusively for businesses, for commercial and professional purposes (B2B). By submitting a request or paying for services (even if payment is made from a private individual’s personal account), the client confirms that they are acting for business purposes, and consumer protection law does not apply to the relationship between the parties.
   If any provision is invalid or unenforceable, the remaining provisions stay in force, and the invalid one is replaced by a valid provision that comes closest to its purpose.
2. **Information on the website**
   The information on this site — service descriptions, case studies, indicative timelines — is for information only and is not a binding offer. We confirm the exact scope, price and timeline after the brief.
   The website and its content are provided “as is” and “as available”. We do not warrant that the information is complete, current or error-free, or that the site is available without interruption.
   The figures in case studies come from specific projects and do not guarantee the same results in yours.

3. **Requests, estimates and proposals**
   A request through the site, a message in a messenger or a brief creates no obligation for either of us.
   Estimates and proposals are based on the information from the brief and remain non-binding until a contract is signed. Unless a proposal states otherwise, it is valid for 30 days.
   If after the brief the task turns out to be noticeably larger or smaller than described, we will revise the estimate before work begins.
4. **How a project runs**
   The usual sequence:
   - Brief — we discuss your business, the task, timeline and budget, and give a preliminary estimate.
   - Proposal — we fix the scope of work, stages, deliverables, price and timeline.
   - Contract — we sign the contract and, where needed, a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) and a data processing agreement.
   - Prepayment — you pay the advance for the first stage in the amount set in the contract; work starts once it arrives.
   - Stages — we work stage by stage and show interim results; for advertising, SEO and social media a stage is usually one month with a report.
   - Acceptance and revisions — you review each stage, and we make revisions to the extent expressly agreed in the contract or estimate.
   - Handover — we hand over the result, source files, access and instructions.
   Each side names a contact person who makes decisions on the project. Day-to-day questions, approvals and formal notices can go by email or through Telegram, WhatsApp or the project’s work chat (section 18).
5. **Fees and payment**
   The price, currency, payment terms and deadlines are set out in the contract. Larger projects are split into stages: you pay an advance for each stage and the balance after it is accepted, not the full amount up front.
   Third-party costs are not included in the price unless the contract says otherwise: advertising budgets, domains, hosting, paid services and APIs, and licences for fonts, photos and plugins. You pay them directly to the provider or we pass them on at cost. Wherever possible, such services are registered in your name.
   Work beyond the agreed scope is estimated separately and starts only after you approve the new estimate and timeline in writing.
   If payment is late, we may pause work and withhold handover of results until it arrives; deadlines move by the length of the delay.
   Taxes and bank fees are allocated as stated in the contract.
6. **Payments, cancellations and refunds**
   A prepayment reserves our team’s time for your project. Once work on the stage it covers has started, the prepayment is non-refundable.
   Fees for stages that have been completed or accepted, and for service periods that have already begun, are non-refundable.
   If you cancel a project, you pay for the work done up to the date of cancellation — a stage in progress in proportion to the work completed, but not less than the prepayment for it once work has started — plus third-party costs we have already incurred or committed to on your behalf. Any amount you paid beyond that is refunded.
   Advertising budgets and third-party fees (domains, hosting, licences, paid tools and services) are not refunded by us: they are paid directly to the provider or passed on at cost, and any refund is governed by that provider’s terms.
   Subscriptions and monthly retainers (for example, ad management, SEO or social media) can be cancelled with effect from the end of the current paid period. The period already started is not refunded, in whole or in part.
   Where a refund is due, we make it to the original payment method within a reasonable time, and no later than the law requires.
   Please send any payment dispute or refund request to us first — by email to the address published on this website or in your contract or through a messenger (section 18) — and give us 14 days to resolve it before starting a chargeback or payment reversal.
7. **Acceptance and revisions**
   We hand over the result of each stage for your review. You review it within the period set in the contract or, if none is set, within 3 business days.
   Please send your comments as one consolidated list — by email or in the project’s work chat. Comments must be reasoned and concern whether the result matches the original brief.
   Revision rounds are included in the price only if, and to the extent that, they are expressly set out in the contract or estimate. Any work beyond the expressly agreed scope, and any change to the original inputs, is charged separately (clause 5.3).
   If the client sends no reasoned comments within the scope of the original brief during the review period (or, if none is set, within 3 business days), the stage is deemed accepted in full and without reservations. Starting to use the result — publishing the site, launching the ads — also counts as acceptance.
8. **Timelines**
   Stage deadlines are set in the contract and run from the moment the prepayment has arrived and we have the materials and access we need. They are target dates unless the contract expressly calls them binding.
   While we wait for materials, answers, access, decisions or payment from you, deadlines move by the waiting time. If the project is on hold for reasons on your side for longer than the contract allows (or, if it says nothing, for more than 30 days), we may invoice the work done so far and resume the project on a new schedule.
9. **What we need from you**
   To keep the project on track, the client:
   - provides the materials, information and access needed for the work on time (texts, logos, photos, access to the website, ad accounts and CRM);
   - names a contact person and gives feedback within the agreed time;
   - holds the rights to everything it gives us (texts, images, trademarks, databases) and has a lawful basis for sharing its customers’ personal data with us where the project needs it;
   - is responsible for the accuracy of information about its product, prices and promotions, and for the product and advertising claims complying with the law and platform rules;
   - keeps its own backups of websites, accounts and data;
   - pays for the work and third-party costs on time.
   The client indemnifies us against third-party claims, fines and reasonable legal costs arising from materials, data or instructions it provided, or from its products, offers and advertising claims, unless the claim was caused by our fault.
10. **Intellectual property**
   Exclusive rights to results created specifically for you (designs, layouts, code, texts, creatives) pass to you once the relevant stage or project has been paid in full. Until then, the results may be used for review and evaluation only.
   Together with the rights, we hand over the source files and materials listed in the contract.
   Our own pre-existing or independently developed assets (libraries, components, templates, scripts, internal tools, methods) remain ours. To the extent they form part of the result, you receive a perpetual, royalty-free, non-exclusive licence to use them strictly within your own project — without the right to extract them from the product, copy, replicate, sublicense or resell them to third parties.
   Open-source components and third-party materials (fonts, stock photos, plugins, services) are used under their own licences; paid licences are registered to you or charged as expenses (clause 5.2).
   We may mention our work together and show non-confidential results in our portfolio unless you object in writing or the contract or an NDA prohibits it.
11. **Confidentiality**
   Everything you tell us about your business — data, figures, plans, access credentials — is used only for the project and never disclosed to third parties, except contractors who need it for the work and are bound by the same obligations.
   On request, we sign a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) even before the brief.
   This obligation applies during our work together and for 1 year after it ends, unless the contract or NDA sets a different period. It does not cover information that is publicly available or that the law requires us to disclose. Confidentiality does not prevent us from using, in our further work, the general experience, know-how, ideas and technical solutions gained while working together.
   We process personal data in line with our Privacy Policy and, in client projects, also under a data processing agreement.
12. **Results, platforms and AI**
   All services — marketing, advertising, SEO and GEO, social media, development, automation and design — are provided on a best-efforts basis, without any express or implied guarantee of return on investment, sales, leads, conversions, traffic, rankings, visibility in AI answers, uninterrupted operation, merchantability or fitness for a particular commercial purpose. Outcomes depend on factors outside our control: the market, your product and prices, competitors, budgets and the algorithms of search engines and AI systems. Specific figures are binding only where the contract expressly sets them as guaranteed KPIs.
   Any decisions and actions of Google, Meta, TikTok, Telegram, app stores, hosting providers, domain registrars, AI providers and any other third-party platforms — moderation, ad and app rejections, shadow bans, account restrictions and suspensions, changes to rules, algorithms, prices or APIs, and outages — are entirely outside Veilvex’s responsibility and are not grounds for a refund or compensation. Help with such issues beyond the agreed scope is additional paid work.
   We are free to use AI-based tools and neural networks at any stage of the work — for research, copy, images, code and automation. We do not guarantee that a result will pass third-party AI-content detectors, and we are not responsible for outages, API changes, restrictions or decisions of third-party AI models and services.
13. **Completion of acceptance and further support**
   The result is reviewed strictly at the acceptance stage (section 7): the client raises all comments on it within the review period.
   Once a stage or project has been accepted — including automatically when the review period expires or when the client starts using the result — Veilvex’s obligations for that stage are deemed fully performed, and the result is delivered “as is”, without any warranties.
   Any later changes, fixes, updates, support and further development are carried out only for a separate fee or under a separate support contract, unless the individual contract expressly provides otherwise.
   We are not responsible for how the result works after changes made by the client or third parties, after misuse, or after updates to hosting, browsers, platforms, third-party components or services.
   To the extent the law allows, no claims are accepted in respect of an accepted stage or project; cases in which liability cannot be limited by law are governed by clause 14.4.
14. **Limitation of liability**
   To the extent permitted by law, our total liability arising out of or in connection with a contract, whether in contract, tort or otherwise, is limited to the fees you paid for the specific stage or service that gave rise to the claim during the 3 months before the event giving rise to it.
   We are not liable for indirect or consequential losses, lost profits, revenue or business opportunities, loss of goodwill, or loss or corruption of data, nor for the acts and omissions of platforms and third-party services.
   Where we breach an essential contractual obligation through slight negligence, our liability is limited to the foreseeable damage typical for this type of contract.
   None of these limitations applies to intent or gross negligence, fraud, injury to life, body or health, mandatory product liability, or any other case where the law does not allow liability to be limited or excluded.
15. **Force majeure**
   Neither party is liable for delays or non-performance caused by circumstances beyond its reasonable control: natural disasters, armed conflict, sanctions and other acts of government, large-scale failures of communications, power grids or cloud platforms, and attacks on providers’ infrastructure.
   A party affected by such circumstances informs the other without delay, and deadlines move for as long as they last. If they last longer than 30 days (or the period set in the contract), either party may terminate the contract; the work done up to that point is paid for.
16. **Termination**
   The contract may be terminated on the grounds and in the manner it provides. If the contract does not cover this, either party may terminate it with 14 days’ notice given by any of the means in section 18.
   Payments and refunds on termination follow section 6.
   Completed and paid-for results are handed over to you together with the rights to them (section 10).
   We may pause work or terminate the contract with immediate effect if payment is overdue by more than 14 days (or the period set in the contract), if the task would require breaking the law or platform rules, or if the client otherwise materially breaches the contract.
17. **Governing law and disputes**
   The governing law and the way disputes are resolved are set by the contract with the client. If the contract does not specify them, the law of the country where our contracting party is registered applies.
   We first try to settle any dispute by negotiation: send your claim by any of the means in section 18, and we will reply within 30 days. If we cannot agree, the dispute is heard by the courts at the place of registration of our contracting party, unless the contract provides otherwise.
18. **Notices and language**
   Correspondence in Telegram, WhatsApp and the project’s work chats between the contacts of the parties’ representatives has full legal force, on a par with email sent to the address published on this website or in your contract — including for agreeing the brief, additional work and estimates, handing over stages, accepting work, claims, cancellations, termination, refund requests and other formal notices. “In writing” in these terms includes such messages.
   A message is deemed received when it is delivered to the contact of the other party’s representative — as given in the contract, on the website or used in project correspondence. Each party is responsible for access to its own accounts and gives notice of any change of contacts. Requests about personal data can also be sent in the ways described in the Privacy Policy.
   These terms are published in English, Russian, Azerbaijani and German. English is the default language of this website: if the language versions differ, the English version prevails.
19. **Changes to these terms**
   We may update these terms. The current version and its date are published on this page.
   A signed contract is governed by the version in force on the date of signing, unless the parties agree in writing to switch to a newer one.
20. **Contact**
